title: Frittata di Asparagi
subtitle: Spring asparagus frittata with parmesan
excerpt: Frittata di asparagi is a flat Italian omelette made with lightly cooked asparagus spears and parmesan. The asparagus is blanched first so it keeps its shape and colour inside the set egg, and the parmesan adds the only seasoning the dish needs beyond salt.
sourceNotes: Asparagus frittata is a spring staple across northern and central Italy, where white and green asparagus are cultivated widely. The Veneto region is particularly known for its asparagus dishes, including the frittata. The dish is one of the classic uses for fresh asparagus at the start of the season.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Blanch the asparagus ahead. Make the frittata fresh and serve warm or at room temperature.

content.text: This frittata showcases fresh asparagus: blanched briefly so it stays green and tender, then set into beaten eggs with parmesan. The asparagus spears sit whole inside the frittata so each slice shows them in cross-section. It is a spring dish and depends on fresh asparagus; there is no worthwhile version with tinned or jarred asparagus.
Heat the grill to high. Bring a pan of salted water to the boil.
Blanch the asparagus for 2 to 3 minutes until just tender. Drain and lay on a clean tea towel to dry. If the spears are very long, cut them to fit the diameter of your pan.
Beat the eggs with the parmesan, salt, and black pepper.
Heat the olive oil and butter in a 24 to 26 cm ovenproof frying pan over medium heat. Arrange the asparagus spears in the pan in a single layer, pointing in the same direction.
Pour the egg mixture over the asparagus. Lower the heat to medium-low and cook for 8 to 10 minutes until the base and sides are set.
Transfer to the grill and cook for 3 to 4 minutes until the top is just set and pale gold. Cool for 5 minutes, then slide onto a board and cut into wedges.

Asparagus frittata is a spring dish from northern and central Italy. The Veneto and Emilia-Romagna regions grow a great deal of asparagus and the frittata is a common use for it. The Veneto also grows white asparagus, which is milder and less bitter than green. Either type works here; white asparagus may need an extra minute or two in the blanching water.
